Here is what was done: both census records — the 1860 Salt Lake County household listing a Joseph Pratt aged 38 with his wife Ann and children Sarah and young Joseph, and the 1880 listing of the same couple now with their adult son Joseph — were matched with high confidence (similarity score 0.78 on each, well into the strong range) to the four Pratt family members already in the tree. The name, birth year, and birthplace all agreed exactly across both records and the tree's established data. The move from Cranfield, Bedfordshire, England to Utah was accounted for by a documented corridor of Latter-day Saint converts emigrating from Great Britain to Utah in that era, described on the FamilySearch Utah emigration wiki page. All 18 assertions are now linked: 20 person-evidence entries in total, with both sides of the wife and son relationship assertions in the 1880 record linked as required. Sarah Pratt is absent from the 1880 census — at roughly 33 years old she most likely married and was enumerated under her husband's surname, but she may also have died or been recorded elsewhere, and that question remains open.

The next step is to search for Sarah Pratt's post-1860 records — a marriage or later census — to find where she went after leaving the household, and then to confirm the established identities through a proof summary for the open question about whether these households are the subject's family.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

**1. Missing required check lines.** The rationale omits:
- A date check comparing the record's birth/age-derived year to the tree person's birth year with the gap stated. a_012 from the same record gives birth year 1845, the tree records ~1845 — gap 0 years — but this is never stated.
- A residence check comparing the record's place and year to the nearest attested residence before this record. The death is in Schuylkill County, 1908; the tree's last attested residence is also Schuylkill County (from the 1860 census). This strongly supports identity, but is not stated.

**2. The rationale uses relationship content as identity evidence.** The line "Names Thomas Flynn as father" reports the substance of a_013, not evidence that the deceased is I1. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

output.text_response:
Here is the subagent's report:

---

**No warnings on I1.**

**Materialization note:** All 14 links are `speculative` because of the birth year conflict. The tool requires at least `probable` or `confident` to materialize sourced facts onto an existing tree person — so I1's tree record does not yet show the new facts (occupation, residence, naturalization, immigration). Those facts will land once you resolve the birth year and the links can be upgraded.

---

Both records were linked to Hermann Gaetjen in the tree, but only as "only possibly" matches.

- The **1875 San Francisco voter register** (src_001) shows Hermann Gatjen, age 21, born in Germany, working as a fireman on Cook Street, naturalized 13 Aug 1875 in the California 4th District Court.
- The **Germans to America index** (src_002) shows Herm Gaetjen, born Prussia 1854, arrived New York 2 Jun 1871.

The two records almost certainly describe the same person: the name is identical (Gatjen/Gaetjen are the same Low German surname spelled two ways; "Herm" is a standard abbreviation of Hermann), birth year from both converges on about 1854, and the trajectory — arriving in New York in 1871, established in San Francisco by 1875, before his eldest child was born there in 1878 — fits neatly. There is a small puzzle in the naturalization: someone arriving in June 1871 would not normally be eligible until 1876 under the five-year residence rule, yet the register records August 1875 — roughly ten months early — and nothing in the project file explains that shortfall.

**Why only "speculative":** The family tree records Hermann's birth as "about 1859" with no source attached, while both records consistently give about 1854 — a five-year gap the rules require to be flagged until formally resolved. Because the links are speculative, the records' facts (birthplace Germany/Prussia, SF fireman, 5 Cook Street, naturalization, 1871 arrival) have **not yet been copied onto Hermann's tree profile**.

**Next step:** If you correct Hermann's tree birth year to **about 1854** — which is what both records say and is almost certainly right given the "about 1859" figure is unsourced — that removes the conflict, allows the links to be upgraded to "probably," and lets all the new facts flow onto the tree profile.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Both records were matched to **Hermann Gaetjen (I1)** and linked at "probably the same person." No separate stub was created. Here is a summary of the findings:

---

## Identity Decisions

**src_001 (1875 San Francisco Great Register — Hermann Gatjen, 21, b. Germany, fireman, naturalized 13 Aug 1875)** → linked to **I1**
- "Gatjen" is a recognized spelling variant of "Gaetjen." Hermann was in San Francisco — exactly where he needed to be, given son Henry Joseph's birth there in 1878. Scored 0.43 (moderate confidence).

**src_002 (Germans to America Index — Herm Gaetjen, b. 1854 Prussia, arr. New York 2 Jun 1871)** → linked to **I1**
- Low index score (0.006) is explained entirely by the thin tree profile and by the conflict with I1's unsourced 1859 birth estimate. When read alongside the Great Register — which independently gives the same 1854 birth year — the two records corroborate each other. No separate stub warranted.

---

## Issues Flagged for Follow-up

1. **Birth-year conflict on I1**: Both records consistently give birth ca. **1854**, while the tree's current "about 1859" is unsourced (from the FamilySearch collaborative wiki). These two birth facts now coexist on I1. → **Conflict-resolution is needed** to retire the unsourced 1859 in favor of the evidenced 1854. A coherence warning currently flags the 1871 immigration as appearing *before* the 1859 birth.

2. **Naturalization gap**: The 2 Jun 1871 arrival gives only ~4 years 2 months before the 13 Aug 1875 naturalization, ten months short of the five years required by law. The shortfall may reflect a transcription error in the arrival date, an earlier undocumented stay in the US, or a court irregularity. → Suggested follow-up: locate the actual 4th District Court naturalization record (FamilySearch collection 2125028, California County Naturalizations).

---

**Recommended next step:** Conflict-resolution to adjudicate the two birth values on Hermann Gaetjen so the coherence warning clears and the tree reflects what the evidence shows.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

---

---

**What the evidence tells us:**
The two records fit together as one immigration story — Herm Gaetjen arrived in New York from Prussia in June 1871, made his way west, and by 1875 was living in San Francisco working as a fireman, where he naturalized that August. Both records consistently give a birth year around 1854. The match was held at "probable" rather than "confirmed" because:
1. The surname appears in three slightly different spellings (Gaetjen / Gatjen / Herm Gaetjen) — common Low German orthographic variants, not different names.
2. Both records say ~1854, but the tree currently carries an unsourced "about 1859."

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

---

Both records were matched to Hermann Gaetjen, the husband and father in your tree. The 1875 San Francisco voter registration shows him living at 5 Cook Street, Ward 9, working as a fireman, and naturalizing as a U.S. citizen on August 13, 1875 — three years before his first child was born in San Francisco. The Germans to America index shows a Herm Gaetjen (almost certainly an index abbreviation of Hermann) born in Prussia in 1854, who arrived in New York on June 2, 1871, and presumably made his way west from there. The two records fit together neatly as a single immigration story, and both are linked to Hermann as "probably" the same person. The match was held at "probably" rather than "certainly" for two reasons: the surname is spelled slightly differently across the records (Gatjen / Gaetjen / Herm Gaetjen are common Low German spelling variants rather than different names), and both records give a birth year around 1854, while the tree currently says "about 1859" — a discrepancy that is not a dealbreaker because the tree date has no source behind it at all and two records consistently say otherwise. There is now a conflict on the tree between those two birth years that needs to be resolved, almost certainly by retiring the unsourced 1859 estimate in favor of the records' consistent 1854.

The next step is conflict-resolution to decide which birth year stands on the tree — the unsourced "about 1859" or the records-derived "about 1854" — and to note that the naturalization happened about ten months earlier than U.S. law normally required, which the original court record may explain.

The 1875 census record (assertion a_001) records a boy named **Anders Pedersen** — born ~1868 in Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway. The only candidate in your tree is **Anders Hansen** (I1), also born ~1868 in Ringsaker, with his father documented as **Hans Olsen** (I2).

Which option would you like to proceed with?
